usage: Subject particle 이 marks the body part that hurts — the default clinic line
삐다 takes 을/를: you sprain a specific joint
Romance-drama staple; note 을, you grab the wrist itself
One word: 손목 + 시계 (時計, 'time-meter') — the watch, not the body part
examples: 손목이 좀 아파요.
My wrist hurts a little.
Simplest clinic sentence — body part + 이 + 아파요
마우스를 오래 써서 손목이 너무 시큰거려요.
My wrist really aches from using the mouse too long.
시큰거리다 = a dull, repetitive joint ache, the desk-job complaint
넘어질 때 손으로 바닥을 짚다가 손목을 삐었어요.
I sprained my wrist when I braced my fall with my hand.
real injury story: 짚다(brace) → 삐다(sprain), past 삐었어요
nuance: 손목 is the wrist joint, built transparently from 손(hand) + 목(neck) — Korean treats it as the 'neck of the hand,' the same logic behind 발목(ankle). The key contrast is with bare 손: 손 is the whole hand, so if you specifically twisted or strained the joint you must say 손목, not 손, or a Korean pictures the palm/fingers instead. Register is plain and neutral — fine for friends and equally fine at the 정형외과(orthopedic clinic), where 손목이 아파요 and 손목을 삐었어요 are everyday lines. Habitual collocations: 손목이 시큰거리다(aches), 손목에 무리가 가다(gets strained), 손목을 삐다/접질리다(sprain). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle on 삐다: English says 'sprain my wrist,' so learners reach for 손목에, but 삐다 takes the object marker — 손목을 삐었어요.

Using 에 with 삐다 by analogy to English ('sprain in my wrist'): it is 손목을 삐었어요 with the object marker 을, not 손목에 삐었어요.
Calling the watch 손목 — the body part is 손목, the watch is 손목시계.

usage: The #1 ankle complaint; object marker 을 on the joint
접질리다 = a sharper 'rolled it' nuance than 삐다
Idiom: literally 'grab the ankle' = drag down / be a burden
examples: 발목이 좀 부었어요.
My ankle is a bit swollen.
Note the ㅅ-irregular: 붓다 → 부었어요, never 붓었어요
계단에서 발목을 삐어서 절뚝거리며 걸었어요.
I sprained my ankle on the stairs and walked with a limp.
절뚝거리다 = to limp — a vivid everyday result of a sprain
내가 실수해서 괜히 팀 발목을 잡은 것 같아요.
I feel like my mistake dragged the whole team down.
발목을 잡다 used figuratively — to hold/hinder, not literal
nuance: 발목 is the ankle, formed as 발(foot) + 목(neck) — the 'neck of the foot,' parallel to 손목. Distinguish it from bare 발(the whole foot): if you rolled the joint, 발목을 삐었어요 is precise, whereas 발 아파요 just means your foot hurts somewhere. It is plain, neutral register and the staple phrase at the 정형외과(整形外科, orthopedics): 발목을 삐다/접질리다, 발목이 붓다/시큰거리다. 발목까지 오는 바지 (ankle-length pants) shows the same word in clothes-shopping. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular, so it conjugates 부어요/부었어요 (drop the ㅅ), and learners wrongly write 붓어요. Second, the idiom 발목을 잡다 means to hold someone back or be a burden — don't read it literally.

Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요 — it is ㅅ-irregular, so the ㅅ drops: 부어요 / 부었어요.
Reading 발목을 잡다 literally as physically grabbing — in most contexts it is the idiom 'to hold back / be a drag.'

usage: Standard clinic phrase; 이 marks the aching joint
to prop oneself on one's elbow
괴다 = to prop up; classic bored-meeting posture
Instrument particle 로: '(by means of) the elbow'
까지다 = skin gets scraped off, intransitive
examples: 팔꿈치가 좀 아파요.
My elbow hurts a bit.
Simplest form — joint + 이 + 아파요
책상에 팔꿈치를 괴고 졸았어요.
I dozed off propped up on my elbow on the desk.
팔꿈치를 괴다 = the prop-your-chin posture; 에 marks where (책상에)
테니스를 친 뒤로 팔꿈치 바깥쪽이 계속 아파요.
The outside of my elbow has hurt ever since I played tennis.
real 'tennis elbow' description with location 바깥쪽(outer side)
nuance: 팔꿈치 is the elbow joint, written as one word from 팔(arm) + 꿈치 with the tense consonant ㄲ. There is no everyday near-synonym — the medical term 주관절(肘關節, elbow joint) exists but nobody uses it in conversation, so 팔꿈치 covers all registers. Habitual collocations: 팔꿈치를 괴다(prop on), 팔꿈치로 찌르다(nudge with — note instrument 로), 팔꿈치가 까지다(scrape), 팔꿈치가 아프다(ache, e.g. tennis elbow). The biggest English-speaker pitfall here is spelling/pronunciation: learners write 팔꿉치 or 팔굼치, but only 팔꿈치 is correct, and you must keep the 팔 — bare 꿈치 is not a word. A second trap is the particle on 찌르다: you nudge 'with' the elbow, so it's 팔꿈치로, not 팔꿈치를.

Dropping 팔 and saying just 꿈치 — the full word is always 팔꿈치.

usage: 찧다 = to bang hard against something; object marker 을
새끼 = the smallest/baby one; the toe you stub at night
사이 = the gap; where 무좀(athlete's foot) starts
examples: 발가락이 아파요.
My toe hurts.
Plain base sentence
신발이 작아서 발가락이 꽉 끼어요.
The shoes are small so my toes feel cramped.
꽉 끼다 = packed/cramped tight — shoe-fitting vocab
밤에 문턱에 새끼발가락을 찧어서 눈물이 났어요.
I stubbed my pinky toe on the door frame at night and my eyes watered.
real-situation: the universal night-time injury, 찧다 in past tense
nuance: 발가락 is a toe, built from 발(foot) + 가락(digit/strand), exactly parallel to 손가락(finger) — once you see the 가락 pattern both words click. Name individual toes with 엄지발가락(big toe, lit. 'thumb-toe') and 새끼발가락(pinky toe, lit. 'baby-toe'). Don't confuse 발가락(toe) with 발톱(toenail): 톱 is the nail, so 'I cut my toenails' is 발톱을 깎다, not 발가락. Register is fully neutral and casual-safe. Typical collocations: 발가락을 찧다(stub), 발가락이 꽉 끼다(toes feel cramped in shoes), 발가락 사이가 가렵다(itchy between the toes). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb for stubbing — English 'stub' has no direct cognate; Korean uses 찧다 (bang hard) with the object marker: 발가락을 찧었어요.

mistakes: Confusing 발가락(toe) with 발톱(toenail) — the nail is 발톱, so trimming nails is 발톱을 깎다.
Misspelling it 발까락 — it is 발가락 with plain ㄱ, even though it sounds tensed.
Reaching for a word like 차다/때리다 to say 'stub' — the natural verb is 찧다: 발가락을 찧었어요.

usage: 굵다 (thick in girth) for limbs — not 두껍다
안쪽 = inner side; back of thigh is 허벅지 뒤
for the thighs to feel tight
당기다 = a pulled/stretched-tight sensation after exercise
examples: 허벅지가 아파요.
My thighs are sore.
Base sentence after any leg workout
청바지가 허벅지에서 꽉 껴요.
The jeans are tight around the thighs.
꽉 끼다 + location 에서 — a real fitting problem for muscular legs
스쿼트를 했더니 허벅지 안쪽이 너무 당겨요.
After doing squats, my inner thighs feel really tight.
당기다 = the post-workout pulled-tight feeling, with 안쪽(inner)
nuance: 허벅지 is the thigh — the thick upper leg above the knee. The contrast to learn is register, not body part: 허벅지 is the normal spoken word, while 대퇴부(大腿部, 'big-leg region') is the clinical/anatomical term you'll only meet in a hospital or textbook — say 허벅지 in real life. Specify regions with 허벅지 안쪽(inner) and 허벅지 뒤(back/hamstring). A vocabulary pitfall for English speakers: 'thick thighs' uses 굵다 (thick in circumference, for cylindrical things like legs and arms), NOT 두껍다 (thick in flat thickness, for books/blankets) — 허벅지가 굵다 is right, 허벅지가 두껍다 sounds off. Other collocations: 허벅지가 당기다(feel tight/pulled), 허벅지가 저리다(go numb), 허벅지 근육(thigh muscle). Also keep it distinct from 종아리(calf), which is the lower leg.

Reaching for 대퇴부 in casual talk — that is the clinical term; ordinary speech is 허벅지.
Confusing 허벅지(thigh, upper leg) with 종아리(calf, lower leg).

usage: for the calf to knot up
뭉치다 = muscle stiffens into a knot
쥐가 나다 = idiom for a cramp; note 에 marks the spot
굵다 for limb girth, not 두껍다
알 = the rounded muscle belly of the calf
examples: 종아리가 아파요.
My calf hurts.
Plain base sentence
하이힐을 신었더니 종아리가 너무 뭉쳤어요.
My calves got really tight from wearing heels.
뭉치다 = knotted/stiff; classic end-of-day complaint
자다가 종아리에 쥐가 나서 깼어요.
I woke up because I got a cramp in my calf.
쥐가 나다 in a real situation; 에 marks where the cramp struck
nuance: 종아리 is the calf — the fleshy muscle on the BACK of the lower leg, the opposite face from 정강이(the bony shin in front); mixing those two is the most common confusion, so anchor it as 'calf = soft back, shin = hard front.' Register is plain and neutral. Its signature collocation is the idiom 쥐가 나다 — literally 'a mouse comes out,' meaning to get a sudden cramp; never translate 쥐(mouse) literally, and note it pairs with the location particle 에 (종아리에 쥐가 났어요). Other habitual phrases: 종아리가 뭉치다(knot up), 종아리가 퉁퉁 붓다(swell up), 종아리 알(the muscle bulge), 종아리 마사지(calf massage). Like other limbs, 'thick calves' is 종아리가 굵다 with 굵다(girth), not 두껍다.

Translating 쥐가 나다 literally — 쥐 means 'mouse' but the phrase just means 'to cramp': 종아리에 쥐가 났어요.
Using 두껍다 for thick calves — limbs use 굵다: 종아리가 굵다.

usage: to get kicked in the shin
차이다 = passive of 차다, '(I) get kicked'
뼈 = bone; the hard ridge you feel up front
examples: 정강이가 아파요.
My shin hurts.
Base sentence
침대 모서리에 정강이를 부딪혀서 멍이 들었어요.
I banged my shin on the corner of the bed and got a bruise.
멍이 들다 = to bruise; 에 marks what you hit (모서리에)
축구하다가 상대 선수한테 정강이를 차였어요.
I got kicked in the shin by the opposing player during soccer.
passive 차이다 with agent 한테 — you receive the kick, not give it
nuance: 정강이 is the shin — the hard, bony front ridge of the lower leg, the exact opposite of 종아리(the soft calf at the back); fix them as 'shin = hard front, calf = soft back.' Because it is bone with almost no padding (살이 없다), knocking it on furniture is a uniquely sharp pain everyone relates to, which is why 부딪히다 collocations are so common. The bone itself is 정강이뼈. Register is plain and neutral. The standout English-speaker pitfall is voice: when something hits YOU, Korean uses the passive — 차이다('get kicked') and 부딪히다('get bumped/knock into'), so 'I got kicked in the shin' is 정강이를 차였어요, and the kicker is marked with 한테/에게. Beginners wrongly use the active 차다('I kick'), which reverses who did it. Note the particle: even in the passive, the shin is marked 을/를 (정강이를 차이다).

usage: to get hit on the back of the head / to be betrayed
Very common idiom; literally 'strike the back of the head'
납작하다 = flat; a real Korean appearance remark
to feel stares on the back of one's head
따갑다 = to sting/prickle; idiom for being watched
examples: 뒤통수가 아파요.
The back of my head hurts.
Plain literal base sentence
선반 모서리에 뒤통수를 부딪혀서 혹이 났어요.
I hit the back of my head on the shelf corner and got a bump.
literal physical use; 혹이 나다 = to get a lump
믿었던 친구한테 뒤통수를 맞았어요.
I got stabbed in the back by a friend I trusted.
figurative betrayal — the most common real use; agent takes 한테
nuance: 뒤통수 is the back of the head, from 뒤(back) + 통수, and it lives a double life. Literally it is where you bump your head (뒤통수를 부딪히다, 혹이 나다). Figuratively, 뒤통수를 치다 / 뒤통수를 맞다 is an extremely common idiom for betraying or being betrayed behind one's back — so in any social context 뒤통수를 맞았어요 almost always means 'I got backstabbed,' not a literal blow. Register is casual; in formal or medical speech you'd switch to 뒷머리 or the Sino-Korean 후두부(後頭部, 'back-head region'). Note also that Koreans genuinely judge head shape — saying someone's 뒤통수가 납작하다(flat) vs round is normal small talk. The pitfall for English speakers is exactly that idiom: don't take 뒤통수를 맞다 literally when the topic is trust, and mark the betrayer with 한테/에게.

usage: 에 marks the spot; 땀이 나다 = sweat comes out
만 하다 = 'only as big as' → idiom for very small
to hide the sky with a palm
Proverb: to try to cover up the obvious
examples: 손바닥이 간지러워요.
My palm is itchy.
Base sentence; 손바닥이 + adjective
넘어질 때 손바닥으로 바닥을 짚었어요.
I braced my fall with my palms.
instrument 으로 = used the palm to brace; 짚다 = to prop
우리 집은 손바닥만 해서 짐 둘 데가 없어요.
Our place is so tiny there's nowhere to put things.
손바닥만 하다 used figuratively for 'tiny' — a cramped apartment
nuance: 손바닥 is the palm — the inner flat surface of the hand, from 손(hand) + 바닥(floor/flat bottom). Its built-in opposite is 손등(back of the hand), where 등 means 'back'; keep the pair 바닥(inner)↔등(outer) straight, since beginners mix them. Register is neutral. The standout idiom is 손바닥만 하다, literally 'only the size of a palm,' used to call something very small — most often a cramped apartment (집이 손바닥만 하다); treat it as figurative, not a real measurement. There's also a well-known proverb 손바닥으로 하늘을 가리다 ('cover the sky with your palm' = futilely hide what everyone can see). Typical collocations: 손바닥을 펴다(open the palm), 손바닥에 땀이 나다(sweaty palms from nerves), 손바닥으로 바닥을 짚다(brace with palms). The pitfall is the instrument particle: you brace 'with' the palm → 손바닥으로, not 손바닥을.

mistakes: Confusing 손바닥(palm, inner) with 손등(back of the hand) — 바닥 is the inner flat side, 등 is the outer back.
Taking 손바닥만 하다 as a literal measurement — it is the idiom 'tiny / palm-sized.'
Using 손바닥을 짚다 to mean 'brace with your palm' — the instrument particle is 으로: 손바닥으로 짚었어요.

usage: After a long day of walking; 이 marks the sole
to get a blister on the sole
물집이 잡히다 = a blister forms (set phrase)
Idiom: feel like they're on fire from walking
examples: 발바닥이 간지러워요.
The soles of my feet are itchy.
Base sentence; 발바닥이 + adjective
새 구두를 신고 발바닥에 물집이 잡혔어요.
I got blisters on my soles from new dress shoes.
물집이 잡히다 = blister forms — never 물집을 만들다
하루 종일 걸었더니 발바닥에 불이 나는 것 같아요.
After walking all day, my soles feel like they're on fire.
불이 나다 used figuratively for burning fatigue
nuance: 발바닥 is the sole — the flat underside of the foot, from 발(foot) + 바닥(floor/flat bottom), mirroring 손바닥(palm). Its opposite is 발등(the top of the foot, where 등 = 'back/upper side'); don't confuse the underside 바닥 with the top 등. Register is neutral, and it shows up constantly after long walks, with blisters, and at the 지압(指壓, acupressure) and foot-massage shops that are popular in Korea. The crucial collocation pitfall for English speakers is blisters: a blister 'forms' or 'is caught' — 물집이 잡히다 / 물집이 생기다, with the blister as the SUBJECT (이/가) — so it's 발바닥에 물집이 잡혔어요, never the English-style 물집을 만들다('make a blister'). Other set phrases: 발바닥에 불이 나다(soles burning, figurative) and 발바닥이 화끈거리다(soles feel hot).

mistakes: Confusing 발바닥(sole, underside) with 발등(top of the foot) — 바닥 is the bottom, 등 is the upper side.

usage: 에 marks the spot; 땀이 나다 = sweat comes out
냄새 = smell; 암내 is the blunter word for body odor
to feel a lump in the armpit
멍울 = lump (e.g. lymph node); 잡히다 = is felt
examples: 겨드랑이가 간지러워요.
My armpit is itchy.
Base sentence; 겨드랑이 + 가 + adjective
여름엔 겨드랑이에 땀이 너무 많이 나요.
My armpits sweat way too much in summer.
에(spot) + 땀이 나다 — Korea's humid summers make this daily
겨드랑이에 멍울이 만져져서 병원에 갔어요.
I felt a lump in my armpit so I went to the hospital.
real-situation health concern; 만져지다 = to be felt by touch
nuance: 겨드랑이 is the armpit/underarm, a native Korean word with no everyday synonym — just memorize the ending -랑이. It is extremely practical in Korea's hot, humid summers for talking about sweat (땀이 나다) and odor; note that neutral 겨드랑이 냄새 is polite, while 암내 is a blunter, more loaded word for strong underarm B.O. that you should use cautiously. It also appears with 제모(除毛, hair removal), deodorant (데오드란트), and—seriously—with health checks, since a 멍울(lump) felt in the armpit can mean a swollen lymph node. The first English-speaker pitfall is spelling: people write 겨드랑or 겨드량이, but only 겨드랑이 is standard. The second is the sweat verb: 'I sweat' is 땀이 나다 (sweat comes out, sweat as subject), never 땀을 하다 — so 겨드랑이에 땀이 나요.

usage: After long sitting; 이 marks the sore part
to settle in and stick with it
Idiom: 'plant your butt' = sit down and persevere
to be slow to get going / a homebody
examples: 엉덩이가 아파요.
My bottom hurts.
Base sentence after long sitting
딱딱한 의자에 오래 앉아 있었더니 엉덩이가 배겨요.
My bottom is sore from sitting on a hard chair too long.
배기다 = a hard surface presses into you — natural office complaint
공부 잘하려면 엉덩이를 오래 붙이고 있어야 해요.
To study well you have to keep your butt in the chair a long time.
엉덩이를 붙이다 = to sit and persevere — a very common idiom
nuance: 엉덩이 is the buttocks/bottom and the general seat-and-hip area. It is an everyday, non-vulgar word: fine in normal conversation, while 궁둥이 is the more childish/casual variant (often used with kids) and the clinical term 둔부(臀部) is hospital-only — default to 엉덩이. Keep it separate from 허리(waist/lower back): seat soreness is 엉덩이, but lower-back pain is 허리 아파요, and English 'I hurt my back/bottom' tempts learners to swap them. Idioms make this word punch above its weight: 엉덩이가 무겁다 ('heavy bottom') = slow to get up or a homebody, and 엉덩이를 붙이다 ('stick your butt down') = settle in and persevere at study or work. Collocations: 엉덩이가 배기다(sore from a hard seat), 엉덩이 운동(glute exercise). The pitfall is the idioms—don't read 엉덩이가 무겁다 as literal weight—and the 엉덩이 vs 허리 split for where it hurts.
